doc.title: Ann Rabson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 21, 2007

title: Choosing other people's songs and writing around 'Stormy Monday'
summary: She does songs with great music more than great words, and wrote her own tune inspired by an overplayed standard.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: What attracts you to do somebody else’s songs?

That’s a really good question. If it’s got great music and okay words I’ll probably do it. If it’s got great words and not very interesting music I’m not doing it. And there have been cases where there was one song, and I’m embarrassed to admit this, well actually it’s happened several times, where there’ll be a song — well I’m not embarrassed — there’s

a song that I really am inspired by the music. I mean I don’t copy the music, but I’m really inspired by something about the music, but the words just do nothing for me. And I’ll take it on and make it my own. Or, another thing is a song that’s done so much that I’m just so sick of playing it and hearing it, like “Stormy Monday” is a good example. Great song. But you know, oh come on. So I wrote another song with a similar feeling and similar changes but I added a minor here and some, what do they call it, altered chords?
And I didn’t know what they were called I just knew I wanted to do them, you know, to change it. But it was inspired by another song.
